title: Asian stocks mixed as CoreWeave lifts chipmakers; hot U.S. inflation weighs
full_text:
Investing.com -- Asian stocks were mixed on Wednesday as semiconductor shares rallied in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, while Hong Kong and Chinese technology stocks came under pressure.
Strong earnings from CoreWeave supported the AI trade, but hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation revived concerns over further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
The MSCI Asia Pacific Index rose as much as 0.8%, extending a recovery that had delivered its strongest two-day advance in more than three months.
Technology shares led the gains, while Nasdaq 100 futures climbed 1.2% and S&P 500 futures added 0.6%, recovering losses in the underlying Nasdaq 100 during regular U.S. trading.
South Korea's KOSPI gained 1.8%, Japan's Nikkei 225 advanced 1.2% and the TOPIX rose 0.8%. South Korean chipmakers led gains, with SK Hynix climbing 3.6%, LG Innotek rising 3.6% and Samsung Electronics adding 2.4%.
In Japan, TDK gained 3.43%, Kioxia advanced 2.99% and Murata Manufacturing rose 2.65%. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing gained 2.63%, while Largan Precision added 2.96%.
Hong Kong's Hang Seng fell 0.9%, while the CSI 300 and Shanghai Composite slipped 0.2%, each. Chinese technology losses were led by NetEase, down 2.6%, MiniMax, which fell 2.6%, and Meituan, which declined 2%. CXMT slipped 0.2%, while SMIC edged up 0.1%.
CoreWeave lifts AI optimism, but inflation revives rate concerns
CoreWeave shares rose around 2% in late U.S. trading after the AI computing provider reported quarterly results above analyst estimates and raised its annual forecast, indicating that demand for computing capacity remains strong despite concerns about constraints across the data-centre industry.
Anticipation also grew around Anthropic's planned listing, with the company targeting a fully diluted valuation of $1.4 trillion.
The optimism was tempered by October U.S. inflation data. Consumer prices rose 0.4% month-on-month, while core CPI increased 0.3%, exceeding expectations for a third consecutive month.
Markets are now pricing in a quarter-point Fed rate increase in December, with some possibility of a larger move, and roughly three quarter-point hikes by June.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said faster increases could be needed over the winter, while Governor Christopher Waller said a 50-basis-point move in December may be warranted.
Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee described the latest inflation report as disturbing. US cash Treasury trading is closed on Wednesday for a public holiday.
China tech weakness reflects more than the U.S. rate outlook
The pullback in Chinese and Hong Kong technology shares reflects the combination of higher US rate expectations and lingering concerns about AI valuations and competition.
Uncertainty over U.S.-China technology cooperation ahead of the November 18-19 Trump-Xi meeting have weighed, while losses in Meituan have been compounded by a broker downgrade.
SoftBank Group fell as much as 11% in Tokyo after reporting a ¥1.12 trillion ($7.1 billion) fiscal second-quarter loss, including a $3.7 billion writedown on its U.S. data-centre projects amid falling AI valuations.
Alibaba said its chip division, T-Head, had confidentially filed for a Hong Kong IPO. The company submitted its Form A1 application on September 11 after receiving exchange clearance to proceed with the proposed spin-off, which would give investors more direct exposure to one of Alibaba's core AI and semiconductor businesses. Alibaba shares nevertheless fell 1.3%.
Other regional benchmarks were mixed. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 0.1%, Singapore's STI gained 0.7%. India's Nifty and Sensex rose 0.2% and 0.1%, respectively.

title: Fed rate hike odds in December at 88% after hot CPI- CME Fedwatch
full_text:
Investing.com-- Markets sharply raised their bets that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates in December following hotter-than-expected consumer inflation data on Tuesday, CME Fedwatch showed.
A swathe of hawkish statements from Fed officials also factored into increased bets on a December hike.
Markets are now pricing in a 88.8% chance for a 25 basis point hike in December, up from about 72% a week ago, CME Fedwatch showed.
Markets are no longer pricing in the possibility of a December hold, and are pricing a 11.2% chance the Fed hikes by 50 bps next month.
Trade the Fed’s rate hike cycle with insights from InvestingPro-- now at 55% off!
The shift in expectations was driven chiefly by stronger-than-expected consumer price index inflation data for October, released on Tuesday.
Headline and core CPI grew faster than expected last month, driven by a mix of high energy costs and pricing related to the artificial intelligence buildout.
The print was accompanied by hawkish commentary from Fed officials on Tuesday. Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank ought to hike rates in December, citing increasing risks from sticky inflation.
Separately, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson– who has a vote on the Fed’s rate-setting board– also said she supported a “further gradual tightening” in monetary policy.
The central bank raised rates by 25 bps in September– its first such move in three years– with Chair Kevin Warsh reiterating the bank’s commitment to its 2% inflation target.
While the central bank did leave rates unchanged in October, analysts questioned whether the hold heralded a steeper pace of tightening in the coming months.
“In hindsight, the Fed’s decision to keep interest rates on hold in October looks to have been a mistake. Or, if the Fed prefers to wait for more data, it could mean that it is prepared to raise rates in larger increments than 25bp when it does act,” ANZ analysts said in a note.
Third-quarter gross domestic product data read stronger than expected, as did nonfarm payrolls data for October.
The prints showed that the two biggest overhangs for further Fed tightening– slowing growth and a weak job market– remained largely in check, giving the central bank enough headroom to consider more rate hikes.

title: Oil prices rebound from 2-mth low as M.east risks persist, U.S. inventories shrink
full_text:
Investing.com-- Oil prices rose in Asian trade on Wednesday, recovering from a two-month low as markets remained focused on any signs of de-escalation in the U.S.-Iran war.
Data signaling a bigger than expected draw in U.S. oil inventories also helped spur some gains in crude.
Brent oil futures for January rose nearly 1% to $92.37 a barrel by 22:22 ET (03:22 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures rose 0.6% to $86.53 a barrel.
Oil had slumped to a two-month low on Tuesday, extending losses amid growing conviction that a Democrat-led U.S. Congress will pressure Washington into ending the conflict with Iran.
U.S. President Donald Trump also signaled restraint on Iran this week, downplaying the need for more military strikes against the country.
An effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, over his handling of the Iran war, largely fell through on Tuesday evening, with House of Representatives Republicans voting down the proposal.
Iran also said earlier this week that there were no ongoing peace talks, even as Trump met with Qatari officials to discuss more mediation.
Three tankers were seen catching fire in the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend. Adding to tensions in the Middle East, Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis remained engaged in fighting this week, with the Houthis targeting a key Saudi pipeline.
But other data showed oil and gas transits through Hormuz reached their highest level since the conflict began in February. Separately, a Reuters survey also showed OPEC production increasing despite disruptions in the Middle East.
U.S. oil inventories shrink more than expected- API
Data from the American Petroleum Industry showed U.S. oil inventories shrank 9.8 million barrels in the week to November 6, much more than expectations for a 1.0 million draw.
The data usually heralds a similar print from official inventory data, which is due later on Wednesday.

title: Oil rebounds as Hormuz shipping attacks blunt hopes for Iran truce
full_text:
By Colleen Howe and Jeslyn Lerh
SINGAPORE, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Oil prices rose on Wednesday from the previous session’s two-month lows, as the market swung between hopes for a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran and concerns about attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
Also on Wednesday, a regional governor said a drone attack caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga by the Baltic Sea in northwest Russia, injuring three workers.
Brent futures climbed $1.04, or 1.1%, to $92.53 a barrel at 0420 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude rose 67 cents, or 0.8%, to $86.71.
Recent data showed little sign of fewer attacks in November, after 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the Middle East war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
"There has been an increase of vessel attacks in the Gulf shipping lanes amidst uncertainty of the diplomacy talks," said June Goh, senior analyst at Sparta Commodities.
"With the US midterms well over and more crude flows out of the Middle East, there seems to be more bearish tones to the oil price."
She added that the top driver for oil is the extent to which Iran will come to the table with US demands to reach a diplomatic agreement.
A tanker was struck northeast of Lima in Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Tuesday. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a separate statement on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on the "unauthorized route" in the strait.
"Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase in flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk," LSEG Oil Research said in a November 10 note.
In the previous session, oil prices initially fell by more than $3 a barrel after US officials downplayed the need for further military strikes against Iran, though some of the losses were clawed back after an Iranian security official said no talks were taking place between the two sides.
Meanwhile, US crude oil stocks rose in the latest completed week, market sources said, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Crude stocks rose by 9 million barrels for the week that ended on November 6, the sources said.
In Russia, oil refining capacity has been reduced by about 30% since late October following renewed Ukrainian drone attacks, industry sources said.
Russian and Ukrainian officials met in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for their first peace talks since February as US President Donald Trump’s envoys launched a fresh push to end the war.

title: Goldman expects additional Fed rate hike in March
full_text:
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Goldman Sachs forecast an additional 25-basis-point US Federal Reserve rate increase in March on Tuesday after hotter-than-expected October inflation data prompted it to revise its expectations of an end to the hiking cycle in December.
The bank is the first among its peers to change its forecast since Tuesday’s data marked a third consecutive month of upside surprises, which now has markets fully expecting a 25-basis-point hike on December 9, per CME FedWatch.
Goldman said a third rate hike is more likely in March than January, as it expects inflation to ease through the end of the year before renewed "start-of-the-year" price pressures amid elevated costs lift inflation again.
"It is possible that by the time of the March meeting, or even the January meeting, the energy shock will feel largely over. But we suspect that the recent inflation readings will lead most FOMC participants to signal a third hike in the December dot plot," Goldman Sachs chief US economist David Mericle said.
The brokerage now expects rate cuts to begin in December 2027, three months later than previously forecast, followed by additional cuts in March, June and September 2028.
Inflation has been supported by rising oil prices amid the US-Israel conflict with Iran, President Donald Trump’s import tariffs, resilient consumer demand and robust AI investment.
Higher living costs added to voter dissatisfaction, contributing to heavy midterm election losses for Trump’s Republican Party last week.

title: Fed officials open door to a quicker round of rate hikes as inflation worsens
full_text:
By Howard Schneider and Ann Saphir
WASHINGTON, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The odds that the Federal Reserve may raise interest rates by half a percentage point next month jumped on Tuesday after US data showed prices rising faster than expected in October and policymakers opened the door to a quicker pace of rate hikes.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% on a monthly basis in October, down from the 0.6% registered in September as energy inflation receded. The core index excluding volatile food and energy prices, however, rose 0.3% for the third month in a row, evidence of persistent underlying inflation and price pressures spreading through the economy.
A few hours before the data was released, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he planned to support a quarter-point increase at the Fed’s December 8-9 meeting unless core CPI came in at 0.3% or more.
"In that case, I believe a 50-basis-point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting," he said at a conference in London hosted by King’s Business School and the Money Macro and Finance Society.
Sticking with a smaller rate increase, Waller said, risked hurting the Fed’s inflation-fighting credibility, given inflation was too high and appeared to be broadening.
Economists polled by Reuters had expected core monthly inflation to drop to 0.2% in October. The CPI data and Waller’s comments drove a powerful selloff in the US Treasury market, with the yield on 2-year notes — a proxy for Fed policy expectations — rising by the most since early April 2025.
By mid-morning, market pricing reflected about a 15% chance of a half-point rate hike before retreating to about 10% in the late afternoon. Over the course of the day, traders also piled into bets the Fed would keep to its usual quarter-point rate hikes but deliver three of them by mid-2027, rather than two as seen before the data.
MORE RAPID MOVE POSSIBLE
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said in separate remarks at an energy conference that it "may be possible to move more rapidly" than the pace implied by the quarter-percentage-point hike approved in September followed by a hold at the following meeting, in October. Logan said she feels the Fed needs to raise rates by at least half a percentage point more before pausing to take stock.
"The goal should be to make policy modestly restrictive so we can sustainably deliver both maximum employment and stable prices," Logan said, noting that the current 3.75%-4.00% policy rate was too low and "adding to inflationary pressures."
Kansas City Fed President Jeffrey Schmid, who hosted the conference with Logan, said inflation is "top of mind" for him and that he too believes the central bank’s policy rate is "fairly accommodative." He asked attendees to think of themselves as Fed policymakers and to indicate whether they felt the Fed should cut, hold steady or raise rates in December; none picked a cut, and a large majority picked a hike.
"Isn’t that kind of interesting? And I think it’s actually instructive," he said, adding that a big part of his job is to demystify what the Fed does, including how it makes rate-setting decisions.
ONGOING INFLATION RISKS
The October inflation data followed US midterm elections last week that revolved around cost-of-living issues and ended in a rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
The October data showed unexpected jumps in the cost of auto insurance, public transportation and medical services, increases that could land particularly hard on middle- and lower-income households. Policymakers see those groups as the weak link in an overall solid consumer spending picture.
"There was not much in today’s report to assuage concerns about ongoing inflation risks or the fact that the Fed will need to hike rates further to tamp down price pressures," Omair Sharif, president of Inflation Insights, wrote after the release of the CPI data.
He said the data put the core Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index on track to rise 0.34% in October, which would translate into a 4% annualized pace and represent an increase from the prior month. The Fed uses the PCE Price Index to measure progress toward its 2% inflation target, but it considers the core figure a better measure of inflation trends.
Fed Vice Chair for Supervision Michelle Bowman said later on Tuesday that she too was worried about persistent inflation, but warned that tighter financial conditions from falling stock prices and higher bond yields posed potential risks to the economy.
She said she expected inflation to cool next year as long as price pressures from the AI buildout and the Middle East conflict abate, and did not sound in a hurry about rate hikes.
"The trend is not on a downward trend for inflation, and I think that that should give us some pause as we think about the need to address inflation and at what pace and on what timeline," Bowman said in Washington at the Council on Foreign Relations. "I would let my colleagues’ statements speak for themselves, but certainly I think I gave an indication today that I think addressing inflation is the right move for us."

title: European shares near record high as earnings absorb tech volatility
full_text:
Investing.com - European shares advanced on Wednesday, pushing the benchmark STOXX 600 within a whisker of a record high, as a resilient corporate earnings season and relief over strong U.S. artificial intelligence demand offset lingering anxiety over a hawkish repricing of Federal Reserve interest-rate expectations.
The pan-European STOXX 600 index rose 0.4%, extending a durable rally as investors cheered a highly constructive third-quarter earnings season.
Germany’s DAX rose 0.9%, while France’s CAC 40 was up 0.7%. London’s FTSE 100 rose 0.8%.
With a vast majority of the index constituents having now reported, solid corporate balance sheets have largely absorbed the recent volatility in global bond and energy markets, giving institutional allocators the confidence to keep cash deployed in continental equities.
The primary engine for Wednesday’s European advance was a distinct relief rally across the technology sector, triggered by robust overnight earnings from U.S. cloud computing provider CoreWeave.
Viewed as a critical barometer for the massive capital expenditures required to sustain the global AI build-out, CoreWeave had recently found itself at the epicenter of investor anxiety regarding AI-related debt and infrastructure sustainability.
However, the company reported better-than-expected revenue and continued strong demand for its cloud services, directly alleviating fears of an imminent spending slowdown.
European semiconductor and enterprise software franchises gained in sympathy, with BE Semiconductor and ASM International jumping over 4% each, while ASML and STMircoelectronics gaining over 3% each.
Markets digest hot U.S. Inflation and 50-bps whispers
Trading desks spent the session digesting the fallout from Tuesday’s hotter-than-expected U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) report.
The robust inflation data definitively shattered hopes for an immediate easing of transatlantic financial conditions, firmly cementing market expectations for at least a 25-basis-point rate hike by the Federal Reserve at its December meeting.
Furthermore, the combination of sticky core consumer prices and last week’s blowout U.S. jobs report has prompted a subset of fixed-income allocators to question whether the U.S. central bank might be forced to consider a bumper 50-basis-point increase to cool resilient domestic demand.
Oil bounces as ECB’s Lagarde takes the Stage
Crude oil prices rose on Wednesday, bouncing from the previous session’s two-month lows. Traders swung between optimism for a diplomatic de-escalation in the conflict involving the U.S., Israel, and Iran, and renewed concerns over physical supply disruptions following fresh attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde is scheduled to deliver remarks later in the day. Bond and equity desks will parse her comments closely for cues on how the ECB plans to navigate the widening divergence between a stalling European economy, fluctuating energy premiums, and accelerating U.S. inflation.

Analysts had forecast a 1.8% decline in fourth-quarter total advertising revenue, within a range of a 5% fall to 0.4% growth. A year earlier, revenue fell 6%.
Third-quarter advertising revenue dropped 8%, ITV said, and the company expects full-year advertising revenue to fall around 2-3% from 2025.
Chief Executive Carolyn McCall said advertising demand in the second half "has weakened" due to broader economic uncertainty, increased digital advertising on global streaming platforms and Less Healthy Food regulations that took effect on Oct. 1, 2025.
The £30 million of temporary savings will align costs with advertiser demand, comprising £25 million in content spending and £5 million in discretionary non-content costs.
ITV expects its total content budget for 2026 to be about £1.2 billion.

ITV said the decline was slightly worse than its previous guidance due to economic uncertainty.
Media and Entertainment revenue fell 1% to £1.43 billion, below the £1.44 billion forecast, which implied no change, as 7% growth in digital revenue to £461 million was offset by a decline in traditional television advertising.
Streaming hours rose 29%. The unit’s non-advertising revenue fell 3%, compared with a forecast decline of 4%.
Group revenue fell 1% to £2.76 billion, against a forecast of £2.77 billion. External revenue declined 2% to £2.36 billion, compared with expectations of £2.37 billion, or a 1% fall.
ITV Studios revenue fell 1% to £1.33 billion, in line with forecasts. External revenue fell 4%, compared with an expected decline of 3%, reflecting the anticipated timing of production deliveries and licensing deals, which are heavily weighted towards the fourth quarter.
Organic revenue at the studios unit fell 1% in the nine months, compared with 7% growth a year earlier.
ITV maintained its expectation of good full-year revenue growth at the unit, ahead of the market, with an EBITA margin at the lower end of its 13-15% range.
The sale of ITV’s Media and Entertainment business to Sky is progressing as planned, the company said.
The Secretary of State issued a Public Interest Intervention Notice on Nov. 4, and ITV expects the deal to be completed in the second half of 2027.
Net debt stood at £695 million at Sept. 30, compared with £652 million at June 30.

title: German October inflation eases to 2.8% as expected; core slows to 2.1%
full_text:
Investing.com -- German inflation eased to 2.8% in October, as expected, while core price pressure cooled more sharply to 2.1% from 2.4%, final data showed on Wednesday, with a new fuel discount masking still-elevated energy costs.
The reading matched the 2.8% forecast and confirmed the provisional result from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). Inflation was 3.3% in September and 2.9% in August.
Consumer prices fell 0.2% from September, in line with the forecast of -0.2%. The harmonised index of consumer prices rose 2.8% from a year earlier and fell 0.1% from September.
Energy prices were 12.2% higher than in October 2025, after a 14.9% rise in September. Motor fuels rose 28.9% year on year, versus 37.1% in September, with the fuel discount in effect since Oct. 1 likely to have dampened the increase, Destatis said.
Heating oil prices rose 84.5% from a year earlier, versus 74.9% in September. Electricity prices were -5.2% and natural gas excluding operating costs -1.2% versus a year earlier, partly due to federal government measures taken since the start of the year.
Energy prices fell 2.1% from September, with motor fuels at -5.5% in particular following the new fuel discount, while heating oil rose 4.6%.
Inflation excluding food and energy was 2.1% in October, against 2.4% in each month from July to September. Inflation excluding energy was 2.0%, and excluding heating oil and motor fuels it was 1.7%.
Service prices rose 2.5% from a year earlier, with net rents excluding heating expenses up 1.9%. Goods prices rose 3.0%. Food prices rose 0.4%, the same as in September, with eggs up 15.4% and butter at -18.9%.
Destatis President Ruth Brand said, “The persistently high rate of inflation continued to be primarily driven by the development of energy prices, even though the new fuel discount introduced at the beginning of October is likely to have dampened inflation somewhat.”

title: Bitcoin falls below $74k as hot CPI data spurs rate hike bets
full_text:
Investing.com-- Bitcoin fell on Wednesday, pressured chiefly by increasing conviction that the U.S. Federal Reserve will hike interest rates further in the coming months to quell sticky inflation.
Broader cryptocurrency markets also remained on the backfoot amid increasing uncertainty over the U.S. regulatory outlook, after the Democrats won majorities in both chambers of Congress.
Bitcoin fell 1.2% to $73,935.0 by 00:56 ET (05:56 GMT).
The world’s largest crypto hit a three-month low in overnight trade, pressured by a stronger dollar and yields. Capital outflows from spot exchange-traded funds continued into this week, also adding to pressure on prices.
Rising rate hike bets pressure Bitcoin after hot CPI
Markets ramped up their expectations for a December rate hike after consumer price index inflation data read hotter than expected for October.
The print was accompanied by hawkish commentary from two Fed officials, who also called for higher rates to combat higher inflation.
Markets are now pricing in a nearly 89% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, and a small chance for a bigger, 50 bps hike, CME Fedwatch showed.
The tool showed markets had largely reversed all bets that the Fed will stay on hold in December.
Higher rates bode poorly for risky, speculative assets like crypto, given that they increase the opportunity cost of investing in the sector over debt.
Bitcoin has historically underperformed in high-rate environments, as seen during the Fed’s hiking cycle in 2022-2023.
The prospect of higher rates added to Bitcoin’s woes, with the crypto already nursing losses from last week after the Democrats swept both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.
Markets feared that the Democrats will call more regulatory scrutiny in the industry, given that they have historically pushed for tighter anti-money laundering and risk management practices in crypto.
Crypto price today: altcoins drop tracking Bitcoin
Broader crypto prices largely retreated on Wednesday.
World no.2 crypto Ether fell 2.4% to $2,066.29, while XRP fell 3.8%.
Solana and Cardano fell 3.5% and 2.3%, respectively, while BNB fell 1.4%.
Among memecoins, Dogecoin fell 2.8% and $TRUMP rose 0.4%.

title: German growth stronger than expected, seen picking up: Bundesbank chief
full_text:
FRANKFURT, Nov 11 (Reuters) - German economic growth will accelerate this quarter as Europe’s largest economy recovers faster than expected, even if deep structural challenges continue to hold it back, Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said on Wednesday.
Germany, the world’s third-biggest economy, has stagnated for most of the past three years as its vast industrial sector lost some of its competitive edge. A recovery has started to take hold this year, and a surge in government spending on defence and infrastructure has given it an additional boost.
"Our interim assessments point to a stronger recovery than we were expecting in the summer," Nagel told a conference in Riga. "Economic growth is likely to accelerate in the fourth quarter."
In June, the Bundesbank forecast economic growth in 2026 would be just 0.5%, but most major forecasters now see a growth rate of more than twice that and expect it to hold up in the coming years.
The real surprise this year was the recovery of manufacturing, especially chemicals and electrical equipment output, and order levels suggest that this trend is likely to continue, Nagel said.
"However, the recovery is not yet broad-based," Nagel added. "Private consumption remains subdued, and investment in machinery and equipment declined in the second quarter."
Nagel also noted that the potential growth rate of Germany remains especially low and deep structural changes are needed to lift this.
The country needs labour market reforms as its working age population is shrinking, it needs to work on transitioning its energy sector to carbon neutrality and must find ways to foster stronger private investment, Nagel said.

title: Foreign investors pull out $50 billion from Asian equities in October on AI, cash burn woes
full_text:
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Foreign investors pulled nearly $50 billion out of Asian equities, the largest monthly outflow in four months, in October as concerns over hyperscalers’ cash burn and fears of tougher AI regulations ahead of US midterm elections triggered a selloff in regional tech-linked stocks.
These investors withdrew a net $49.77 billion from equities in South Korea, Taiwan, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam and the Philippines — the largest monthly net outflow since June — according to LSEG.
Democrats’ victories in last week’s US midterm elections, including in states where opposition to new data centres has grown, kept those concerns alive.
So far this month, foreigners have offloaded a further $22.6 billion from these markets.
"The outflows reflect a retreat from AI-linked positions amid increased doubts about AI infrastructure spending and profitability," said Wael Makarem, lead financial market strategist at brokerage firm Exness.
"Ahead of the US midterm elections, tighter environmental reviews and regulations were seen as hindering data centre construction and chip demand."
Foreign investors sold a net $30.68 billion of Taiwanese stocks last month, the most since at least January 2008, and a net $14.59 billion of South Korean shares.
So far this month, the two markets have logged further foreign outflows of $19.76 billion and $8.32 billion, respectively.
Some analysts said foreign investors may be pulling money from Asia and reallocating it to developed markets, as the MSCI Asia Pacific ex-Japan index fell 6.91% in October, compared with a 1.69% decline in the MSCI All Country World Index.
"International investors may have been drawn to the relative resilience of the S&P 500 compared to the MSCI Asia ex-Japan during the month," said Scarlett Liu, Asia-Pacific equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas.
"Additionally, some investors may have increased allocations to US Treasuries as the 10y UST yield rose to 5.3% in early October."
Indian stocks also recorded a second consecutive monthly foreign outflow, totaling $3.6 billion last month. However, cross-border investors have so far invested a net $5.68 billion in local equities this month.
"We upgrade India to overweight as we think it now offers resilient earnings and more reasonable valuations," said Herald van der Linde, head of equity strategy for Asia Pacific at HSBC, in a note on Monday.
Meanwhile, Indonesian and Thai stocks saw outflows of $938 million and $199 million, respectively, while Vietnamese and Philippine stocks recorded inflows of $122 million and $109 million, respectively, last month.

FLSmidth narrowed its organic revenue growth guidance for 2026 to a range of 1% to 3%, compared to the previous range of 0% to 4%. The midpoint of the new revenue guidance of 2% sits below the midpoint of the prior range of 2%.
However, the company’s improved profitability outlook reflects benefits from strong earnings margins in the Service and PC&V businesses and planned improvements in the Products business.
"The third quarter reflected continued good commercial activity, with 32% organic order intake growth and 6% organic revenue growth," said CEO Toni Laaksonen. "We also delivered an improved adjusted EBITA margin of 16.3% and solid cash flow from operating activities."

title: Europe’s STOXX 600 near record high as Siemens Energy, CoreWeave outlooks lift sentiment
full_text:
By Johann M Cherian and Anjana Jayakrishnan Nair
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Europe’s STOXX 600 index opened higher and traded near record highs on Wednesday, as strong forecasts from Siemens Energy and US-based CoreWeave helped ease concerns about the AI trade outlook, while inflation worries kept a lid on gains.
The pan-European index gained 0.7% to 662.83 points by 0807 GMT and was just a whisker away from breaching record levels reached in August.
AI equipment maker Siemens Energy gained 6.5% on expectations of higher profit margins in 2027. The company announced plans to more than triple its dividend.
Shares of its peers Schneider Electric and Legrand gained around 2.6%, while the broader tech sector added 1.7%.
Neocloud company CoreWeave said it would become profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028.
Among laggards on the STOXX index, wind turbine operator Vestas fell 6%, after reporting third-quarter operating profit below market estimates.
Czech-based ammunition and arms producer CSG tanked 18% after cutting its full-year operating margin forecast.
A rebound in Brent crude prices following shipping attacks in the Strait of Hormuz stoked some caution, a day after hotter-than-expected US inflation data lifted expectations for a December interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve.
